terms.comment: Literally “take in hand again”; of mental work, to reconsider, go back over, revise a text or a law. It also means to withdraw, to refuse (Lewis & Short).
Its first sense is to recognise (see recognize); it is also to look over and check: troops, accounts, a text. The editors’ word for revising a book (Morgan–Owens).
To free from faults; especially frequent of correcting what one has written (see reform).

terms.gloss: rework, put back on the anvil
evidence: Hor. A.P. 441: male tornātōs incūdī reddere versūs (M-O s.v. revise)
terms.comment: Horace’s image for reworking badly turned lines; incūs is an anvil.

terms.gloss: a going over again, revision; review
evidence: Lewis & Short: “a retouching, revision”, chiefly in Augustine’s title Retractātiōnēs

phrases.latin: observābō mē prōtinus et, quod est ūtilissimum, diem meum recognōscam
phrases.english: I will watch myself from now on and, what is most useful, go back over my day
Go over this letter again before you send it.

sources: Lewis & Short: retracto · Lewis & Short: recognosco · Lewis & Short: emendo · Lewis & Short: incus
Seneca from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-seneca-epistulae); the other passages as Lewis & Short or Morgan–Owens quotes them.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. revise, rewrite.
